newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says Libya sanctions have gone on too long.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Libya sanctions have gone on too long.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said on Tuesday United Nations sanctions against Libya had been in effect for too long and risked becoming meaningless.

Mubarak brushed aside U.S. criticism that his country was helping Libya and said he hoped the U.N. Security Council and the U.S. administration would reconsider their stance on sanctions against Tripoli.
"The embargo has gone on for too long. When an embargo is prolonged it loses meaning," Mubarak, whose country borders Libya, said in a television interview.
"I spoke to the U.S. administration about this but then they (U.S. officials) say Egypt is helping Libya.

"Libya is an Arab country, it is our neighbour and I have half a million Egyptian workers there. What do they want me to do with Libya? Close my doors? It is an Arab country, I can't. When embargoes go on longer than necessary it makes people explode and we don't want this."
Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi flew to Niger and Nigeria last week in Libyan aircraft, despite a U.N. air embargo against Libya.
The Libyan news agency said Gaddafi visited the two West African countries to hold prayers marking the Moslem new year.
The U.N. imposed an air, arms and diplomatic embargo against Libya in 1992 for failing to extradite two Libyans linked to the 1988 bombing of a Pan-Am airliner over Scotland which killed 270 people.
The sanctions, which were later extended, also penalise Libya for failing to cooperate in an investigation into the 1989 bombing of a French UTA airliner over Niger that killed 171 people.
American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson said on Tuesday Gaddafi had been on a "joy ride" aimed at defying U.N. sanctions and the issue would be taken up by the Security Council's sanctions committee.

Some U.S. officials have in the past accused Egypt of breaking the embargo against Libya but the Cairo government denies this. Egypt was criticised by the United States when Gaddafi violated the U.N. ban by flying on a Libyan-registered plane to Cairo to attend an Arab summit in June 1996.
"I hope the Security Council and the U.S. administration look at this issue in a new way because when it becomes prolonged it leads to explosion," Mubarak said.
Richardson said he had "raised the Libyan issue" during closed-door Security Council consultations on a number of issues.
Council president Park Soo Gil of South Korea said there was agreement among council members to refer the matter to the sanctions committee, which has the same membership as the 15-nation council.
The committee would meet either on Thursday or Friday and seek explanations "by the three countries concerned" -- Libya, Niger and Nigeria -- and establish the facts.
The Security Council issued a statement last month rapping Libya for flying pilgrims to Saudi Arabia in breach of sanctions.
It was the third consecutive year Libya had violated sanctions by flying pilgrims to Jeddah on an unauthorised flight even though the council had authorised EgyptAir to fly the pilgrims.

Libya has offered to allow the two men wanted in the Lockerbie case to stand trial before a Scottish judge under Scottish law at the World Court in The Hague. Britain and the United States have rejected this as unacceptable.
